Surgery is the primary therapy for endometrial cancers that are stage I to III;1-5 oophorectomy is performed, as well as total abdominal hysterectomy, because of the significant incidence of ovarian metastases. No further treatment is required in women with stage I disease who are at low risk of recurrence. In those with stage I disease and a higher risk of recurrence, adjuvant brachytherapy or pelvic irradi- ation are used. In all other women, adjuvant radiotherapy is given, the field being tailored depending on the disease stage. Adjuvant progestogen therapy has not been shown to be effective.6 There are a few studies of adjuvant chem- otherapy in women at high risk of recurrence, but further data from randomised trials are required to assess its role.7 For women with advanced disease (stage IV), systemic therapy with progestogens or cytotoxic chemotherapy can be considered, although response rates are only up to 30%,1,3 and evidence for a survival benefit is questiona- ble.8 Progestogens are likely to be preferred because of their better tolerability. Tamoxifen also produces minor benefit; alternation with progestogens may prolong the re- sponse to hormonal therapy.5 Well-differentiated tumours, long disease-free interval, and positive hormone receptor status are factors that suggest increased response to pro- gestogens. When progestogens are ineffective, chemother- apy may be tried. The drugs of choice are probably doxo- rubicin, cisplatin or carboplatin, paclitaxel, and cyclophosphamide.5,8,9 The combination of carboplatin and paclitaxel has become standard in many centres in the management of advanced or recurrent endometrial can- cer.5,9 Investigational therapies include dactinomycin, go- nadorelin analogues such as goserelin, and anastrozole.3 1.
